metadata.title: From teacher quality to teaching quality: Instructional productivity and teaching practices

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2011 8th-grade mathematics data with a two-stage sampling design (schools, then one class per school) and matrix sampling of test booklets. The analytic sample is restricted to student–math-topic/subtopic pairs for which instructional time is observed and to subtopics taught during the school year (for the main estimates), which is a substantive sample restriction rather than a weighting adjustment. The manuscript does not report applying TIMSS sampling weights or replicate weights, and the empirical strategy relies on student fixed effects with standard errors clustered at the teacher level; therefore, the paper’s estimates should be interpreted as conditional on the selected analytic sample. For replication with TIMSS microdata, analysts should use the official TIMSS student/sampling weights (and replicate weights if available) if the goal is population-representative inference; however, the paper’s identification is primarily within-student across-topic comparisons and may be less sensitive to weighting than to the instructional-time measurement and the taught/untaught subtopic design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are described as TIMSS math test scores at the topic/subtopic level derived from observed student–subtopic responses, and the paper explicitly restricts analyses to observed student–subtopic pairs rather than using PV-based achievement scores. The manuscript does not describe any imputation strategy for missing instructional time or other missing covariates beyond excluding observations with missing instructional time; this is a reporting gap for missing-data handling details. Because the study’s key identification relies on within-student comparisons and on the taught-vs-untaught subtopic structure, the authors’ missing-data approach is likely driven by these restrictions, but the exact rule set is not fully documented.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Primary (U.S.) causal estimates use TIMSS 2011 8th-grade mathematics. The paper restricts to observations for which math instructional time is not missing; the main analysis sample contains 7,258 students across 387 classes in 359 schools taught by 376 math teachers. Outcomes are constructed at the math-topic level (Number, Algebra, Geometry, Data & Chance) using subtopic-level performance scores, but the main estimates focus on subtopics taught during the school year (as indicated by the TIMSS teacher survey), while the falsification test focuses on subtopics not taught during the year. Because TIMSS uses matrix sampling, students within the same classroom receive different booklets; the paper further restricts to observed student–subtopic pairs so that topic/subtopic scores reflect direct performance on items administered to each student rather than imputed aggregate scales.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics (U.S.) — taught vs untaught subtopics falsification test
main_findings.target_variable: Math achievement (topic score) on untaught subtopics
main_findings.performance_metrics: Falsification test (Table 1): Instructional Time (IT) coefficient = 0.000 (SE 0.008) to −0.004 (SE 0.011) across columns; IT*Active Learning index = 0.001 (SE 0.023) to 0.009 (SE 0.024); IT*Assessment = −0.000 (SE 0.018) to −0.008 (SE 0.019). Observations = 22,615.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics (U.S.) the study leveraged student fixed effects, math topic constants, and interactions with the Active Learning index and assessment frequency to predict math achievement on untaught subtopics, finding no relationship between instructional time and topic scores when focusing on subtopics not taught during the year. This indicates that the within-student across-topic instructional-time variation is unlikely to be driven by topic-specific student skills, supporting the credibility of the instructional-time identification strategy.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics (U.S.) — taught subtopics main estimates
main_findings.target_variable: Math achievement (topic score) on taught subtopics
main_findings.performance_metrics: Main estimates (Table 2): IT coefficient = 0.043*** (SE 0.010) to 0.061*** (SE 0.010) across columns; IT*Active Learning index = 0.098*** (SE 0.035) to 0.116*** (SE 0.032) and 0.096** (SE 0.038) in the most controlled specification; IT*Assessment = 0.053** (SE 0.021) and 0.039* (SE 0.021). Observations = 19,038.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics (U.S.) the study leveraged student fixed effects, math topic constants, instructional time, and interactions with the Active Learning index and assessment frequency (plus controls including untaught subtopic scores in the fully specified model) to predict math achievement on taught subtopics, finding that one additional weekly hour of topic-specific instructional time increases math test scores by about 4.3% of a standard deviation on average and that this effect is larger under higher active learning implementation. This indicates that reallocating instructional time toward topics taught with more active, interactive practices may substantially increase the learning gains from instructional time, though the paper’s causal claims rely on the maintained exogeneity assumption rather than ML-based prediction.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics (U.S.) — heterogeneity by AL index percentile
main_findings.target_variable: Math achievement (topic score) productivity across Active Learning index
main_findings.performance_metrics: AL distribution (Table 3): effect of one weekly hour of instructional time on math test scores (in SD units) varies from 0.021 at the 10th percentile (−50% vs median) to 0.056 at the 75th percentile (+33%) and 0.065 at the 90th percentile (+55%), with median (50th percentile) = 0.042.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics (U.S.) the study leveraged the Active Learning index together with the instructional-time effect estimated in the main model to predict math achievement productivity at different points of the AL distribution, finding that instructional time is substantially more productive for teachers at higher AL percentiles (e.g., 0.056 SD vs 0.021 SD per weekly hour from the 75th vs 10th percentile). This indicates that teacher practice profiles can meaningfully condition the returns to instructional time, suggesting that professional development and instructional coaching should target active learning and student-teacher interaction practices to maximize learning gains.

main_findings.target_variable: Math achievement (topic score) on taught subtopics
main_findings.performance_metrics: International replication (Table 6): Instruction Time coefficient = 0.007*** (SE 0.002) to 0.010*** (SE 0.003) across columns; IT*Modern Practices (Active Learning index) = 0.037*** (SE 0.014) in columns (1)-(3); IT*Assessment = −0.003 (SE 0.007) and −0.003 (SE 0.007). Observations = 587,100.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics data across 43 participating countries, the study leveraged student fixed effects, math topic constants, instructional time, and interactions with the Active Learning (labeled 'Modern Practices') index and assessment frequency to predict math achievement, finding a robust positive relationship between active learning implementation and instructional productivity internationally. This indicates that policies promoting active learning practices are likely to generalize beyond the U.S. context, supporting cross-country scaling of teaching-practice interventions to improve the effectiveness of instructional time.

data.outcome_summary: The paper uses TIMSS 2011 8th-grade mathematics data to estimate the causal effect of topic-specific instructional time on student math achievement in the U.S. (main sample: 7,258 students) and to replicate internationally across 43 countries (587,100 observations). The identification strategy exploits within-student variation across math topics taught by the same teacher and uses TIMSS’s matrix sampling and teacher-reported coverage to focus on taught subtopics, with a falsification test on untaught subtopics showing no instructional-time effect. The main U.S. results indicate that one additional weekly hour of instructional time devoted to a math topic increases math test scores by about 4.3% of a standard deviation on average, and the effect is moderated by teaching practices: moving from the 25th to the 75th percentile of the Active Learning index increases instructional productivity (e.g., 0.030 to 0.056 SD per weekly hour). Internationally, instructional time effects are smaller (0.7%–1.0% SD per weekly hour) but active learning remains strongly and positively associated with instructional productivity. Limitations include the absence of reported survey-weight handling and missing-data rules beyond excluding observations with missing instructional time; moreover, the study is not an ML prediction paper, so ML metrics and PV handling are not applicable.
